title: The Bishop’s Dance
transcript: White's brilliant idea is Bishop to a 5, a move that sets up an incredible trap. You see, if black wanted to move the king, it would have to do it on one of these two squares because every other square is defended. But, if he does that, now there's going to be a check with the pawn that would have been up on attack on the black bishop and white would win. So, since the black pawns are stuck, black has to move the bishop. But, if it moves here, there is now going to be a skewer of the king and bishop, and again, this would be winning for white. So, [snorts] instead, black really has to go to h 4. White has to be really precise here. Giving a check wouldn't actually achieve anything. After the black king moves, we can try to walk in with the king and maybe try to win this pawn. But, the black bishop is always going to stand in our way, and this position is just actually a draw. But, white is not that naive, and he's going to maintain the initiative by attacking the black bishop with the king. And now, the question becomes, where is the bishop going to go? These squares are defended by the king. This one is defended by the pawn. This one is defended by the bishop. We saw that going here would allow a skewer, and the same thing applies to going to this square. There's going to be a skewer from the other side of the board. So, is this it? Is black simply lost? Well, not exactly. Black can actually go back to e 1. And now, in this position, it is white to move, and so the king doesn't have to be misplaced, allowing the discovered attack. But, realizing that white having the move is the problem, we can find a solution to this position and play the very precise king to h 3. A quiet, but deadly move, simply passing the move back to black. The bishop cannot move to any of these squares. So, black will have to move the king. But, we already know how this goes. White is going to give a check, win the bishop, and the game.
